patches.name: the seaplane runways, turning basin and channels of the Kāneʻohe naval air station
patches.source: Jackson’s chart of 1882, registered; NOAA’s seaplane landing area and fairways; the CUDEM
patches.note: the reefs and reef flats Jackson’s survey of August 1882 draws inside today’s seaplane landing area, the fairways to the air station and the Crashboat Channel, where today’s sea floor lies deeper than 3 m: cleared for the seaplane runways, the turning basin and the channels, laid back at 1 m deep, where the reefs of 1882 that still stand round the south bay are (the median of their tops; the pack holds no sea shallower). Dredging began with the dredge B. F. Dillingham on 27 September 1939 and went on for three years (11,000,000 cubic yards) “until 1943”; given 1943. The natural lagoon between the reefs, which Jackson sounds at 6 to 8 fathoms, stays as it is; the chart’s registration (about 40 m) leaves the cut a texel or two short of or past the old reef edges

patches.name: the air station’s fill on Mōkapu
patches.source: the fill unit, cut with the 1882 shore of Mōkapu
patches.note: land today that the geologic map calls fill and Jackson’s survey of 1882 shows as sea or reef flat: the airfield’s ground west of Pali Kilo and the strip along Mōkapu’s south shore from the seaplane ramps east to the bay side of Nuʻupia, made with the spoil of the dredging (162 acres west of the runway and about 118 along the south shore, 280 in all, “until 1943”). The 1927 and 1938 maps draw the same shore within about 30 m, so the fill is the Navy’s. Fill over the ponds of 1882 (the causeways of Nuʻupia, Halekou and Kaluapuhi) stays land, as the features draw the ponds

patches.name: Holmes’s fill round Moku o Loʻe
patches.source: Moku o Loʻe’s outline on Jackson’s chart of 1882
patches.note: today’s land of Moku o Loʻe outside the island Jackson draws in 1882, which the 1927 map draws the same: the coral, sand and earth Chris Holmes laid on its reef in 1934–36, doubling its 12 acres, and the later walls and fill of the Navy’s rest station and the marine laboratory, which the sources read do not separate from his; given 1936. The fill unit does not map it

sources.licence: quoted for its dates; a publication of the air station
sources.note: pp. 24–25 (in the Internet Archive’s full text): “On Sept. 5, 1939, workers began building a dike preparatory to filling with material dredged from the Kaneohe Bay”; the dredge B. F. Dillingham began on 27 September; “Dredging and filling continued on the new Naval Base until 1943. By then workers had added 280 acres”, about 118 of them along the south shore from the hangars east, and “West of the runway a dike was built and 162 acres were added to the ancient Heeia section”

sources.title: Building the Navy’s Bases in World War II, vol. II, ch. XXII, Hawaiian Area (Bureau of Yards and Docks, 1947; HyperWar transcription)
sources.licence: public domain (U.S. Navy)
sources.note: Pearl Harbor: dredging for a turning channel round Ford Island from May 1940, the lochs deepened for moorings, Kuahua extended with the spoil from 47 acres to a 116-acre peninsula, Ford Island enlarged by seven acres for its T-wharves. Keʻehi: a dredge brought into the lagoon in February 1943 for three seaplane runways “1,000 feet wide by three miles long”, the spoil raising the land to ten feet. Kāneʻohe Bay: from September 1939, three years of dredging for the seaplane runways (11,000,000 cubic yards)
